extracted.intended_audience: Supreme Court Justices and clerks; patent litigators and patent prosecutors (software/computing arts)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and legal standards for evaluating whether computer-implemented inventions are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, focusing on the Alice/Mayo framework, Diehr, Benson, Flook, and relevant Federal Circuit practice. Includes doctrinal history and examples of how courts treat improvements to computer functionality versus abstract ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory scope of § 101
rubrics_metrics.description: 35 U.S.C. § 101: 'Whoever invents or discovers any new and useful process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter, or any new and useful improvement thereof, may obtain a patent therefor.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Congress intended broad scope ('anything under the sun that is made by man'). This is the baseline: processes, machines, manufactures, compositions, and improvements are potentially eligible subject matter subject to judicial exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial exceptions to § 101
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts recognize exceptions to § 101 for 'phenomena of nature, though just discovered, mental processes, and abstract intellectual concepts' and similar 'fundamental' principles (Le Roy; Benson).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These judicially-created categories—laws of nature, natural phenomena, and abstract ideas—are not patentable. Examples include mathematical algorithms and fundamental economic practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice/Mayo two-step framework
rubrics_metrics.description: Step one: determine whether the claims at issue are directed to one of the patent-ineligible concepts; Step two: if so, ask 'what else is there in the claims' — whether the claim elements transform the nature of the claim into a patent-eligible application ('inventive concept').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts must follow the two-step inquiry from Mayo/Alice, considering elements both individually and in combination. Alice cautions that step two looks for elements sufficient to ensure the patent in practice amounts to 'significantly more' than the abstract idea itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step one — directed to an abstract idea?
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the claim is 'directed to' an abstract idea (historically this has encompassed business methods and mathematical algorithms) or to an improvement in computer/technical functionality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim is properly characterized as a 'basic concept' (e.g., collecting, storing, transmitting data; business practices; mental steps; purely mathematical operations), it will often trigger step one. Courts have tended to list many computing activities as 'abstract' absent a showing of a technical improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step two — inventive concept / 'significantly more'
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim is directed to an abstract idea, assess whether claim elements, individually and in combination, provide an 'inventive concept' that transforms the abstract idea into a patent-eligible application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The inventive concept requires more than the performance of well-understood, routine, and conventional activities previously known in the industry. Generic computer implementation, or use of standard hardware components, normally does not supply 'significantly more.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider claims as a whole; avoid improper dissection
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must be considered 'as a whole' rather than dissected into old and new elements and ignoring the old (Diehr). Courts should not import novelty into the § 101 analysis by dissecting the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diehr holds that dissecting claims into old/new and treating the mathematical part as if it were in the prior art is improper. Alice states its approach is consistent with considering all elements both individually and in combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine-or-transformation test is a useful clue, not sole test
rubrics_metrics.description: The machine-or-transformation test (whether a process is tied to a particular machine or transforms an article) is 'useful and important' but not the sole test for process patent eligibility (Bilski).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts may use the test as a clue to eligibility but must apply the broader Alice/Mayo framework and consider other indicia of a technical improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement to computer functionality or other technical field is eligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventions that 'improv[e] the functioning of the computer itself' or 'effect[] an improvement in any other technology or technical field' remain patent-eligible under Alice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When claims are directed to a specific technical improvement in computers (e.g., new data structure, new way to organize memory, faster/simpler processing) courts have found eligibility (Enfish, DDR Holdings, Finjan). Drafting to articulate a concrete technological improvement supports eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic computer components alone do not confer eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Reciting conventional computer components (e.g., 'data processing system,' 'communications controller,' 'memory,' 'processor,' 'network') is insufficient to render an abstract idea patent-eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functional recitation of generic hardware that performs conventional functions is treated as 'purely functional and generic.' Cases: Alice; Mortg. Grader; buySAFE; TLI. Claims should not rely on boilerplate computer hardware language as the inventive concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pen-and-paper (mental steps) test
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claimed steps can be performed mentally or with pen and paper, the claimed invention is likely an abstract idea (OpenTV 'pen and paper' test).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Showing that a human with pen and paper could perform the claimed steps is evidence the claim is not a technical improvement but an abstract concept; courts use this as a practical indicator in step one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preemption concern as § 101 rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: A core purpose of the judicial exceptions is to avoid preemption—preventing a patent from monopolizing basic tools of scientific and technological work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a claim would effectively monopolize an abstract idea or basic practice (e.g., all ways of performing a business method or basic data-management concept), courts are more likely to find it ineligible. Preemption is the animating concern behind the exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question of fact whether elements are 'well-understood, routine, conventional' (Berkheimer)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether claim elements (or their combination) are well-understood, routine, and conventional is a question of fact; factual findings relevant to eligibility must be proven by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Berkheimer means courts cannot resolve some § 101 challenges on the pleadings or purely as a matter of law when there are factual disputes about conventionality. However, disclosure of a feature in a prior art reference does not automatically mean it was 'well-understood, routine, and conventional.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Limiting to a specific field or adding post-solution activity does not save an abstract idea
rubrics_metrics.description: Limiting an abstract idea to a particular field of use or adding token post-solution steps (e.g., performing on a computer, applying to a specific industry) does not make the concept patentable (Flook; Bilski).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that merely restrict an abstract idea to a technological environment or append conventional post-solution activity are insufficient under Alice step two; courts view such limitations as immaterial unless they supply a technical improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty/obviousness (§§ 102/103) are generally distinct from § 101
rubrics_metrics.description: The novelty of elements (or the overall invention) is 'of no relevance' to the § 101 inquiry according to Diehr; § 101 is about subject matter eligibility, not novelty or obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although related doctrines can overlap in practice, courts must avoid conflating § 101 with § 102/103. However, lower courts and PTAB decisions sometimes reference novelty/prior art in assessing conventionality at step two—this area is contested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims directed to data-management or other high-level functional concepts are vulnerable
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that broadly claim concepts like 'receiving, storing, transmitting, comparing, deleting, and restricting access to data' without a concrete technical improvement are often characterized as abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have repeatedly found that high-level data-management functions, even when implemented with hashing or identifiers, are abstract when the claim merely applies known techniques to generalized data-management goals (TLI; Bridge & Post; decisions invalidating 'content-based identifier' applications).

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal Circuit inconsistency and need for clarifying principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Post-Alice, lower courts—especially the Federal Circuit—have applied the Alice/Mayo framework inconsistently, expanding the list of technologies considered 'abstract' and varying panel-to-panel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document emphasizes that clear guiding principles from the Supreme Court are needed to restore predictability. This affects how practitioners evaluate and draft claims and how courts review eligibility questions.
